title: Installing Packages
description: How to install and manage NuGet packages using the CLI, Visual Studio, and Rider.

data.text: The .NET CLI is the most portable way to manage packages: it works on Windows, macOS, Linux, and in CI. Visual Studio and Rider wrap the same commands in a UI, so anything you do by clicking ends up as a `PackageReference` in the project file.

data.title: Install, pin, and remove
data.content: Install a package, optionally pinning an exact version, then remove it when no longer needed.
data.code:
# Install the latest stable version
dotnet add package Microsoft.Extensions.Logging

# Pin an exact version (recommended for reproducible builds)
dotnet add package Microsoft.Extensions.Logging --version 8.0.0

# Remove a package
dotnet remove package Microsoft.Extensions.Logging

data.title: Inspect the dependency graph
data.content: List what is installed, including transitive packages, and find outdated or vulnerable ones.
data.code:
# Direct and transitive packages for each project
dotnet list package

# Include transitive dependencies
dotnet list package --include-transitive

# Packages with a newer version available
dotnet list package --outdated

# Packages with known vulnerabilities
dotnet list package --vulnerable --include-transitive

data.text: Package sources and the Visual Studio console

In Visual Studio, **Manage NuGet Packages** and the **Package Manager Console** produce the same result. The console equivalent of `dotnet add package` is `Install-Package`; it defaults to the package source selected in the UI.

data.title: Package Manager Console (Visual Studio)
data.content: The PMC uses PowerShell cmdlets instead of the dotnet CLI.
data.code:
Install-Package Microsoft.Extensions.Logging -Version 8.0.0
Update-Package Microsoft.Extensions.Logging
Uninstall-Package Microsoft.Extensions.Logging

data.title: Pin versions in applications
data.text: A floating version such as `Version="8.*"` can pull a different build on a colleague's machine or in CI. Applications should pin exact versions (or use Central Package Management) so restores are reproducible. Libraries often leave the version to the consumer and use `VersionOverride` or a minimum version.

data.title: Directory.Packages.props
data.content: In multi-project solutions, manage versions in one file instead of repeating them in every .csproj.
data.code:
<!-- Directory.Packages.props at the repo root -->
<Project>
  <PropertyGroup>
    <ManagePackageVersionsCentrally>true</ManagePackageVersionsCentrally>
  </PropertyGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageVersion Include="Newtonsoft.Json" Version="13.0.3" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>

<!-- Each .csproj now omits Version -->
<!-- <PackageReference Include="Newtonsoft.Json" /> -->

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use `dotnet add package` (CLI) or `Install-Package` (PMC) to add references
`dotnet list package` shows direct, transitive, outdated, and vulnerable packages
Pin exact versions in apps for reproducible builds
Central Package Management keeps versions in one file across a solution
data.takeaway: Picking a consistent install workflow and pinning versions prevents the classic "works on my machine" restore problems.
